1. The animation compares two illustrative homeowners, Leo and Tessa. It uses Freddie Mac weekly mortgage survey rates to show how a loan's own interest rate relates to the choice between paying down the house and holding cash or investments. Each person has a short bar for their loan's rate, a house, and a stack of gold coins. The captions say "your bar = your loan's own rate" and "your stack = how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit."

2. Mostly the on-screen text changes. A new caption line is added in each frame. By frame 6 the text ends with "a dollar in the house is hard to get back." Within the frames I can see, the pictures barely change. A small pointer appears at Tessa's house in frame 1, and the house and stack shading shifts slightly. Tessa's rate bar sits higher than Leo's, and her coin stack is taller. The frames don't show any numbers or any movement over time.

3. The animation seems to say that the right choice depends on your own loan's rate, and on the gap between 15-year and 30-year offers, rather than on one rule for everyone. It also says money put into the house is illiquid, so it's hard to get back. The footer reads "US only · history, not a forecast," and every label says "ILLUSTRATIVE." So the figures are examples based on past data, and they don't predict future returns.

4. A viewer wouldn't get a clear instruction. The most they could take away is a set of things to weigh: compare your own loan's rate with what else you could do with the money, and remember that extra payments into the house can't easily be withdrawn. The frames don't say "pay extra" or "invest," and they give no break-even rate.

5. The animation's on-screen text suggested the points in answer 4, specifically the "your own rate" framing and the "hard to get back" line. The conclusion that there's no clear instruction is my own reading of what the frames leave out. I haven't added a recommendation for your $320,000 loan, because the image doesn't give enough to support one.
